title: Diagnose and eliminate onboarding drop-off between sign-up and first cohort session by Fri 4 Dec
description:
Users who sign up on zedu.chat occasionally abandon the workspace before inviting members or hosting a live call. Qualitative discovery is needed to remove setup friction and turn registrations into active weekly cohorts.

Work under this goal:
- Deploy the approved 5-question non-sales interview kit to sign-ups who did not finish onboarding.
- Conduct at least 10 user feedback chats to record specific screen-level UX obstacles.
- Deliver a ranked report of the top 3 setup blockers with concrete Next.js UI recommendations.

Done when: 10 interviews are completed with transcripts, and a prioritized onboarding improvement spec is submitted to the engineering team.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Find the step where most sign-ups stop from existing events, then interview 10 people stuck at that step
acceptedWorkstreams.description: The app already sends sign-up, login, page-visit and success events to webhooks (src/utils/webhook-request.ts in Cybertron-HNG/zedu-fe, cybertron-integration, 22 Oct 2026), and onboarding runs through the /auth pages and /[org]/welcome. Plan: 1) with the team, pull those events for recent sign-ups and count how many reach each step (verified account, organisation created, first invite, first channel, first Buzz), so the interviews target the step that loses the most people instead of guessing; 2) recruit 10 of those people with the approved 5-question kit (a team member runs the calls, with consent) and keep transcripts; 3) rank the top 3 blockers with the screen and file that causes each and a concrete UI change. Tasks: funnel count from existing events (research), 10 interviews and transcripts (research), ranked blocker spec (content).

Counting real drop-off from those events before interviewing is the right order.

This goal explicitly requires ten user conversations/transcripts and the accepted approaches already combine funnel-event evidence, interviews, invite-path tests and ranked fix cards. Use a walkthrough inside the accepted diagnosis to generate interview hypotheses; do not label presumed stuck points as observed user abandonment.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Test the invite path with 10 real invites, from send to first message
acceptedWorkstreams.description: The goal says people abandon the workspace before inviting members, but no current approach tests the invite itself. Invite email is the one step where a deliverability problem looks exactly like a product problem. Method: (1) with the team, send 10 real invites from a test workspace to mailboxes the team controls across Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and a school domain, and record the send time, sender name, whether each lands in inbox or spam, and the link; (2) open every invite on mobile and desktop, record each step from click to joining the right channel, whether login is required, and any error (expired link, wrong workspace, no permission); (3) test one expired and one already-used invite; (4) deliver a table per invite (arrived, inbox/spam, steps, failure) and the three fixes with a re-test plan. This connects to the email-authentication work already underway, where DKIM signing is not yet proven, so deliverability must be measured rather than assumed. Tasks: invite delivery test (research), invitee join-path audit (research), fix spec and re-test (content). Nothing is sent to anyone outside the team without consent.

upvotes.reason: Specific deliverable with a clear scope, a named owner for the result and a way to verify it was done properly.
Tests the actual invite path, including spam placement and expired links, which is a distinct and measurable cause of drop-off before members join.

upvotes.reason: This tests whether invitations reach inboxes and whether the join link works on mobile and desktop, which isolates delivery and access failures that interviews may miss. The team-controlled test mailboxes keep it measurable without contacting prospects.

Tests the invite step, the one the goal names and no other approach covers, with 10 real invites across Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and a school domain. It records inbox versus spam and each step on mobile and desktop.

Onboarding drop-off is best diagnosed from what real invited users actually hit between send and first message; ten real invites produce observed stuck points instead of guesses, which is exactly the evidence the fix-list tasks will need.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Turn the diagnosis into a ranked fix list, each item with effort and the sign-off it needs
acceptedWorkstreams.description: The diagnosis locates where sign-ups stop; the drop-off goal only ends when the friction is actually removed. Approach: for each confirmed stop point, write one short fix card: what the screen does today, the proposed change, how hard it is (copy, layout or product change), and what approval it needs from the team. The team then takes the ranked list straight into decisions. Tasks: fix cards per step point (content), effort and ownership pass (research).

upvotes.reason: "Turn the diagnosis into a ranked fix list, each item with effort and the sign-off it needs" is a specific deliverable for this goal with a way to check it was done properly. it produces something checkable rather than an opinion, so the goal either moved or it did not.

The goal ends in a prioritised improvement spec, and fix cards with effort and sign-off needed give the team a direct decision list. It relies on the diagnosis being finished first, but fits the definition of done.

The two accepted approaches find where new users get stuck and test the invite path; ranked fix cards turn those findings into changes the team can decide on. Effort and sign-off make the next work clear and keep recommendations tied to evidence.

The goal ends with a prioritised onboarding improvement spec for engineering. Turning each confirmed stop point into a fix card with effort and sign-off needed is exactly that deliverable, and it is checkable one card at a time. It depends on the two accepted diagnosis workstreams, so it extends them rather than repeats them.
Ranking onboarding friction points by development effort and impact provides engineering with an actionable, prioritized sprint backlog.
